utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we've got your timetable for this week. Bearing in mind the particular witnesses that you're calling are dealing with a very narrow issue, I hope you have more witnesses than this available for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, the witnesses that I have listed have come to The Hague. There is the possibility of -- namely, if you consider that we will get through those witnesses before Friday, there is the possibility that the witnesses which were scheduled for next week could come in this week, but I think that the witnesses I have on the list for this week will take up until the end of the week. I don't think there'll be any gaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps we might review this by the end of Tuesday, but I did say to you I would prefer to have some witnesses sitting around enjoying the delights of the Netherlands weather over the weekend than for us to be sitting down doing nothing. We do want to keep going. So by tomorrow afternoon we'll see how your proposed timetable is going. I know that Mr. Groome has been very long with your client, but, then, he is the defendant, and I would not expect him to be otherwise, but I hope that he won't be nearly so long with anybody else. And I suspect that the nature of the evidence that these witnesses are giving is something which can be dealt with, with all the detail necessary, within a fairly short time, but let's see how we go. Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, you understand, do you, you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you took before we adjourned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You did promise it won't be very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I expect to be finished today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You were talking about something like an hour, I thought you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would have to check the -- review the record to see exactly what I said, but I imagine I would be a bit more than an hour. Your Honour, I'm going to begin with referring to the pseudonym sheet. I don't know if the Court has them handy. I have some extra copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. The accused will need one because they don't seem to let him keep it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have some additional copies for the Court if it requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. It might be just as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I would like to begin today by going back to Exhibit D22, and that is the list that you wrote on your second day of testimony, and you told us that you would prefer to refer to these people by a code number rather than use their name when you testified about them. Now, some of the names on that list we have not heard you tell us about, how it is they fit into this story, and I would like to ask you that now. VGD11. I'd ask you to look at D22. Can you tell us, how is it that VGD11 fits into your account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I will explain this to you. If I may, may I just make some comments with respect to the statement, for example, of -- I can't see it. I apologise. I can't find that particular person. If I may, Mr. Prosecutor, may I make some comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet will have an opportunity to ask you some questions to clarify any matter. What I'm asking you now is with respect to VGD11. Do you have Defence Exhibit 22 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it is VGD11 -- what part does he play in your account of what happened in matters related to this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VG11 is [redacted] and I will tell you something a little bit later on, but I would have to do so in a closed session or private or whatever you call it, but as [redacted]. [redacted]. So I don't wish to mention the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, that's fairly obvious, if he said he didn't want to speak about them in public. If you want him to speak about them, he'll have to speak in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me just ask one question to see if it is necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the information you want to tell us about these two men, does it have anything to do with the matters that are now before the Court or is it some other information?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing with respect to VG10, but I could say something with respect to VG11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Recognising that, I would ask then that we go into private session to discuss VGD11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you just said something that I want to clarify what you meant on the record. And in -- with respect to person number 21, VGD21, you stated the following: "21 gave me that and he told me to set the house on fire." What house are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said that I had set the house on -- he gave me a cassette and the house was at Bikovac. On the cassette, that's what it says. That's what it says on the cassette, and he was mentioned, and number 20 -- 20 and 21, that they had taken part in the execution of Muslims at Rogatica. That's what it's about. And it also -- that is to say the Muslim says how Milan Lukic brought them in and they were beaten and looted and all that kind of thing. And then at the end of that cassette, the reporter, the journalist in the programme says, and another mass crime took place in Visad at the place called Bikovac where Mitar Vasiljevic, Momir Savic, and Zoran Sekulic set fire to a house full of Muslims. That's what it says, the reporter says on the cassette, and that's how I learnt about the house at Bikovac, through that programme and cassette of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've just told us that VGD17, 18, and 19 were police officers that were suspended from the police force. Are they among the group of police officers that were taken into custody with VGD10?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only, not only -- no, 19 wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So 17 and 18.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you a couple of questions about your criminal record. You testified on direct examination that you were arrested and spent six months in gaol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what exactly it was that you did that you were convicted of?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were singing national songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where, exactly were you, when you were singing these nationalist songs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Koritnik. We went to a shop, we drank and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that the songs that you were singing would be intimidating or frightful to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't frightening. Let me tell you this too, yes, we did sing those songs but we weren't singing what -- and they testified to this later on -- they made this seem more serious. That's why we were given prison terms. Otherwise, the songs -- you weren't allowed to sing those songs in the socialist system either, and those didn't harm anybody and I could have shut up thousands of people, because I worked in cafes and restaurants, for singing similar songs but I didn't do that to anyone, whereas me and the five of us or, rather, two of us because the rest were minors, they had -- they went to gaol for 12 days but the two of us went to gaol for six months and me for five.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said that it was in front of a store. Was that store owned by Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't in front of a store. We left the village. It was when we went to Livade, and the shop was socially owned. There was no private property at the time, it was socially-owned shop as we used to call it. They were all socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, did the police observe you engage in this conduct or did Muslims or did somebody make a complaint against you to the police?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of them did report it. And the postman brought us notes, and we went to the police station, and the magistrate sentenced us to two months. We received a summons by the -- from the postman. Then we went to the regular court and were given five months, and the two months that we had already spent in custody were deducted from the final sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Muslims, or at least a Muslim, reported your conduct to the police. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it sounds from your comments here this morning that you feel that your sentence was unduly harsh for the conduct that you engaged in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: The court is the court, and the court makes its decisions. Later on, it was even more dangerous to do something like that, and the sentences were even harsher later on. So perhaps as we were first offenders, that was a mitigating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to read you the charge that you were convicted of and ask you a question. "Article 119: "Whoever with propaganda or otherwise provocates or fans national, racial, or religious hatred or discord between the peoples and nationalities living in Yugoslavia shall be punished with severe imprisonment of up to 12 years." So in fact, you could have received a sentence of up to 12 years for the crime you were convicted of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a crime, it was songs. And nobody was ever sentenced that much for songs. You'd have to do something far more drastic to merit a 12-year sentence. You'd have to be working against the state. But this was just singing under the effects of alcohol. We had been drinking. I don't know how to explain this to you. I couldn't have got 12 years. How would I get 12 years for something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now move to what happened on Pionirska Street. Now, you are very familiar with the allegations against both yourself, Milan Lukic, and some of the other men. And in your statement of the 16th of November last year, you stated that you believed the allegations against Milan Lukic were true. Do you still believe that those allegations are true regarding Milan Lukic as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still do. I always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why is it that you believe that the allegations are true regarding Milan Lukic and his men?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this way: Now they're mentioning me in Pionirska Street. I have now -- not aware of that at all. Let me -- I've already said - let me repeat - I broke my leg on that day. I have no idea that Milan did that, or Bikovac or Pionirska or any of that. I never knew any of that. But witnesses have testified to that. Well, how do I know? They mention him all the time, about the train and about Srebrenica and -- I was present in Sase by the river when the crime took place. In many, many ways he is mentioned. He's mentioned in connection with rape, looting and plundering, killing. Now that they mention me in Pionirska Street and Bikovac. I don't know. I will prove the contrary with respect to Pionirska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've heard a number of witnesses identify Milan Lukic as being present at the actual time that the fire was set on Pionirska Street. Do you believe that any of these people were mistaken regarding Milan Lukic's presence there that night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say? What can I tell you? They place me there. Now, had I been in any way, had I seen, I would have told you. That's as far as I go. Now, I don't want to mention only him, but Sagolje [phoen] as well. But I can't tell you anything about that, anything exact. About 5.00 I broke my leg, and I was not able to be there physically. I was in no condition to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vasiljevic, let's go to the beginning of the day. You've testified that at some point in the day, somebody told you about a horse. Can you tell us who it was that told you about this horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An elderly man, Mimo Ristanovic who lives in Pionirska, up there, too. And my house is close by to the house where the Muslims were, the first time where they looted and plundered them, in that same street nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. He is a neighbour of the person who left, whose horse -- who was the owner of the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would we be able to speak to Mimo Ristanovic today to verify whether or not he told you about this horse on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mimo Ristanovic died. He was an elderly man. I think he died after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A few weeks ago, you told us about Dragan Tomic and how you told him about what happened by the river. Would we be able to talk to Dragan Tomic today to verify whether or not you did tell him what happened at the river?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that Dragan Tomic was killed. His car hit a mine. And the two of them are mentioned. He was the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Ristanovic when he told you --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Visegrad. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Ristanovic when he told you about this horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in town. It happened in town. He asked me whether I know somebody who would take the horse, because nobody wanted the horse. And I said, "Well, I'll come, and we'll take the horse up towards Drinsko and somebody will take it. Somebody needs the horse in rural areas on the farm."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately what time did this conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the person who owned this horse, was it a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had left to Kladanj, I think, or Kakanj perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. He was an elderly man, and all that I know is what he said, that he -- he took that horse often when he went to the mosque, because he was a practising believer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you seen this horse before?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ristanovic, did he give you any details about the horse or did he simply tell you about this horse that had been left behind?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said that the horse was there. "It's a good horse, it's quiet, and it will be good if somebody took it." So something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it your intention to sell the horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no. Nobody'd buy it. And what could I ask for it? I mean, had he been able to sell it, somebody else would have bought it, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to go up and retrieve this horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us more precisely, what exactly was your intention? What were you going to do with the horse once you retrieved it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have taken it uphill. I liked horses when I was a child, and I often rode horses when I was a child. I even broke my head once when I was a child, went to the hospital. And you know, I was born in a village, and I even bought books about horses, about horse training and horse riding for my -- and I worked with horses during summer holidays with my sister and I. You know, those were hard times so that we had to earn some money. And as a child, I worked with horses, and I like horses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, my question is: What was your intention? What were you going to do with this horse once you got the horse? What were you going to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to send it to the village of Drinsko, to take it to the old railway tracks, because there is a lot of grass there. This is an old railway track which was out of use, and I thought that in the village -- in that village there would be somebody who would be willing to take that horse, because in the town, of course, I couldn't find a customer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it was your intention to leave this horse by a set of abandoned railroad tracks, hoping that the horse would walk along those railroad tracks to another village where hopefully somebody would find the horse and take care of the horse? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there any particular reason why you thought that this horse would walk along these railroad tracks?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course when you come out of the inhabited area, because up there, there are meadows and there's woods. People would release horses like that. And especially when I was a child. You could always find horses grazing around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the village that you thought the horse would walk towards, that was a Muslim village in free territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both Muslim and a Serb village. It was a mixed village up there. Drinsko is sort of a neighbourhood community including several villages. Just as you have Prelovo is a neighbourhood community, and there were several villages making a part of it. So Drinsko was a kind of a centre. I mean, there was the local school, the local office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this point in time, were Serbs still living in the village of Drinsko?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbs have always lived there and stayed there. Muslims left the village of Drinsko during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this was a Sunday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this wasn't just any Sunday. In addition to this Sunday being the fourth day of Kurban Bajram for Muslims, it was also an important religious holiday for Serbs, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it was the feast of the Holy Trinity; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there are some Orthodox holidays which are more important than others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean than the Holy Trinity?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you this way: Would it be fair to say that after Christmas and Easter, the feast of the Holy Trinity would be considered one of the most important Orthodox holidays?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't really be able to say anything about that. There are many holidays, Slava for instance, family saints days. There are a number of them. And I think that Holy Trinity is also the family holiday of some people. That is when you take zito to the church. I don't know. I mean, there are people who believe all that or just to offer a sacrifice, to pray so that thunder spares the harvest. I don't know. There are many holidays. I think you are not supposed to build your house that day or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the feast of the Holy Trinity, it's actually a three-day holiday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that on this particular Sunday, most Orthodox Serbs would attend some service in an Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on this holiday, it would be common for Serbs to bring a family icon to the church to be blessed? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Icons? No. You -- when you buy an icon, then you take it to the church. But why would I go from my home to the church carrying an icon? There are icons in the church. Except unless it's been consecrated. You can only take it to the priest to have it consecrated, and you don't need a holiday to do that. You can take your icon for that on any day of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Wouldn't it also be true that a family would prepare a special meal on this particular Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: The -- my family saint is St. George's Day. It is the 6th of May. Yes. You cook special dishes, you invite guests, and so on and so forth. So there are people who -- whose Slava is Holy Trinity. I mean, every family has its own saint's day. So that Holy Trinity is a Serb holiday as such, but there are also families who have taken that as their day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would your wife have cooked a special Sunday meal or meal to celebrate this day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps within the family. But Holy Trinity was not our day, so that we wouldn't have any guests on that particular day. It is a day marked by all Serbs. But I told you that my day is the 6th of May -- or rather, my father. It was my father's Slavs, and when he died, it was my duty to mark that holiday. And when my father was alive, it wasn't my duty to mark that holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've just told us a few minutes ago that on this day, you're not supposed to build your house. Is there a -- are you not supposed to do any work on the feast of the Holy Trinity or is it just house building that is prohibited?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I wouldn't be supposed to do anything, to till the land or build a house. And those are the jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you work on this day, this cleaning of the town that you told us about in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the company, the enterprise you can do, you can work on any holiday, but you can't, you don't do it at the house. We used to work on Christmas day and on once Slava, I mean, we went to work. It's only that at home you are not supposed to do anything, for instance, on Christmas day or Easter or Holy Trinity or Slava. That would be a sin to do anything, to do any work at home, but not when you worked in a company, not when you worked for an enterprise. You've got to go to work. You know, there are so many holidays, nobody would work if companies didn't work on those holidays, and we had to work on holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I'm asking you about the 14th of June, 1992 on the feast of the Holy Trinity, did you work cleaning the town of Visegrad on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've testified that Serbs and Muslims would help you clean the town. Did you clean the town alone that day or did you clean it with other people?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With others, in the company of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were some of those people Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were some of those people Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it is your testimony here that on this day that had religious significance for both Serbs and Muslims, they volunteered to work with you to clean the town; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, I won't say shop owners, people from restaurants, people who worked at the post office or the bank, they always cleaned it. They did it every day. It's not much of a job, I mean you can do it in no time at all, and women -- how much I worked that day, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it's your testimony that both Serbs and Muslims volunteered to work with you on this Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm saying while I was there. Now that Sunday, how many, I can't remember, Serbs and Muslims, I don't know. Perhaps more than Muslims, it was Bajram -- well, there wasn't much need to clean. It wasn't all that much, perhaps in the early days but then the place was -- the town was really put in order so it didn't really have to do much about it later on, you just ask people nicely and they do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your testimony is now that there wasn't much to do that day, and you're not sure whether you had both Muslims and Serbs and how many working with you that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Certainly, there was Serbs, men and women, who were engaged in their regular jobs at work in their shops or restaurants or wherever. So they'd come out, clean each one in front of his own shop and so, day in, day out. It wasn't difficult. As the time went by, it became very easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It sounds from the way you're describing this that on this day you worked in the centre of the town where the shops were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you ever working in the area of Pionirska Street earlier in the day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, we did go there earlier before that but, you know, it was the cleanest area up there because the houses are new there. It's a newly-developed area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you on Pionirska Street cleaning on the day of the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Or, again, I didn't -- I don't -- I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you were here when Witness VG87 told us how he watched you walk along the street, and he told us that he was watching you from the attic of his house. He told us how odd it sounded to him for you to be calling people out to clean the street when, in fact, most of the Muslims had either fled or had been taken away. Does that refresh your memory whether or not you were on Pionirska Street earlier in the day engaged in this cleaning activity?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, no, I don't think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it possible that you were on Pionirska Street earlier in the morning of the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, how can I say exactly? I did rounds of streets, perhaps I did go up there, but I can't tell you exactly. And if I was there, then it had to be earlier, around 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it is possible that you were on Pionirska Street earlier in the day, approximately 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty. Perhaps -- I can't, I mean it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was also that particular witness's belief that what you were really trying to do was to find out whether there were any Muslims remaining in the houses on Pionirska Street. My question to you is: Is it a fact that what you were doing on Pionirska Street earlier on that day was to try to trick the remaining Muslims by getting them to come out of their houses to clean the street? Isn't that what you were doing on Pionirska Street earlier on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To invite Muslims out, to find out how many of them there were and so on, oh, no, sir. No. No. It never occurred to me. Why should I be inviting them out? Why should I be checking on them? I mean, that's what he thinks, that's what he says, well, that's his view. His wife perished there on Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, by your own testimony, it was the -- one of the cleanest areas in town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. It was always the cleanest area of town because it's a new area and there are many houses, but new houses. It was very clean. It was very densely populated, but a newly-developed area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as you have just noted, he is describing what he saw happen on the day that his wife died. You don't think that he's confusing this day with any other, do you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. Perhaps very likely. I don't know what he thinks. How, why does he assume that I wanted to do something? Well, I don't know. That's what he thinks and I cannot really comment about it. I mean, that is what he thinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me if VG87 wanted to tell a lie about you to get you in trouble, he could have told the Chamber that you were present when the fire was started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't say anything about that. That is his opinion, and I have a high opinion of him as a man. I know him. I don't know what he really said, but that is his view but, of course, he must be angry because his wife burned to death there, and there were children too. So that is what he thinks. What can I do about it? That is how I understood him, that he took it that that was the reason why I invited people out. Never. Never in my life, nor did I know what Lukic was about to do. How could I?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you've testified in response to questions by Mr. Domazet that sometimes when you drink, you forget some of the things that you do, and you've also told us that you were drinking on this day. Is it possible that you were on Pionirska Street earlier in the day, calling people to come out to clean and that because you were drinking, you do not have a clear memory of it? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, Pionirska Street wasn't the only one I was on, I did rounds of all streets, a number of streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just referring to the 14th of June. Is it possible that you were up there on the morning of the 14th of June calling out people but have forgotten because you were drinking at the time? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was there, it was not in ill faith, I had no bad intentions except to see that it was -- that it went on to be clean, but that I -- to count the Muslims there, no, out of the question, so that something could be done. So as to do something, well, with them, that is a witness, what the witness says and of course he's angry, that is natural. But I can't really comment much on that. I don't really know what to tell you. All I know is, sir, that I did not participate in any way possible, that I searched people as this lady witness has said, VG13. She mentioned Milan Lukic 16 times, and by then, on the second occasion, she never mentioned the -- she only mentioned Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic and she mentioned herself 16 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you what you were wearing that day. In response to a question put to you by Mr. Domazet, you said that after your cousin's death, you wore dark clothing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, dark clothes, yes, not exactly mourning, but dark clothes. But I think I had olive-green/grey trousers. That was all old. When I came out of the hospital, I did not take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're talking before the hospital, and would it be correct to say that you wore dark clothing as a sign of respect for this cousin that you cared for very much?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you were also --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dark colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were also asked whether or not you owned a black hat and you told us that you do own a black hat. I want to ask you some specific questions about that hat. When you say that the black hat had the brim upturned, I want to ask you, is it the sides of the hat that had a brim that was upturned?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the brim of the hat still stuck out in the front and the back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the brim in the front and the back of the hat, that was not upturned, was it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, just -- this is just a plain hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that if the brim of the hat were allowed to be down, that it would be reasonable for people seeing this hat to mistake it for a cowboy hat?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do I know? It also says that they had a Sajkaca, and that it was a Serb cap. It was a yellow straw hat, and others saw me in a camouflage uniform, some others saw me in olive-green/grey, some others saw me without uniform. How do I really know, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is not about what other people said. I'm asking you to tell us about the hat that you have told us, the black hat that you have told us you own. And my question is: If the sides of the hat, the sides of the brim were allowed to be down, can you tell us how it would be different from a cowboy hat, how would your hat be different from a cowboy hat?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what shall I tell you? I mean to my mind, all hats are the same, cowboy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So in other words, it would not be unreasonable for somebody to see you in this hat and mistake it for a cowboy hat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the hat was imaginary, thought up, because we've heard of a straw hat, a yellow one, somebody saying a cowboy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, please, you have been asked to answer the questions about your black hat. Now, please answer the question and do not keep on talking about the evidence generally. We'll never finish if you keep on like this. You have a very clever counsel here. He will obtain from you anything which he thinks is relevant which you have not been allowed to answer as the witness, but we have got to stop this continual description by you of what other people have said in the evidence unless you are asked specifically about it. Now, Mr. Groome, you are talking about something which I am having a little trouble with. You are talking about a hat with the brim down being mistaken for a cowboy hat. It may be that your idea of a cowboy hat and my idea of a cowboy hat are quite different, but I've always understood, perhaps from watching too many American films, that cowboys wear their hats with the sides of the brims up. Now, you better describe what you mean by a cowboy hat so that he can deal with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You just heard Judge Hunt describe seeing cowboy hats in movies. Have you seen movies with cowboys wearing hats?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how is it that your hat is, this black hat is different from the typical cowboy hat that one might see in a movie? How did it differ?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cowboy hats are usually big. Big, cowboy hats are, they're big.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there any other difference between your hat and a typical cowboy hat?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hat we wore was the classical type of hat, the classical type.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For those of us who are unfamiliar with classical type hats, can you describe other than the size, was there anything to distinguish your hat from a cowboy hat?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The hats that the army wore were turned upwards. Some were black, some were camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it would not be unreasonable for somebody to see your hat and to believe or to describe it as a cowboy hat? Would you agree with me that that is a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Depending on how you see it. Everybody has his own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to go back to the horse. Where were you going to find this horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Vucine, the place is. It's about five minutes, ten minutes away from Pionirska. The same street, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as you came up -- or let me ask you this first: Did you travel to this place up from the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on your way up from the town, did you see any convoys or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you this: I was in town, but I don't remember seeing those people in town at all. They say they were in front of the hotel. Probably, they were. But I don't remember seeing those people at all in town at any moment, any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you just prior to going up for the horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in town. But as I say, I don't remember seeing any of those people. I knew (redacted) from Sase well. But these people -- nothing is clear to me. I didn't see them in town when they went to the hotel. I don't know. None of that -- I remember none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long did it take you to travel from where you were in town up to Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten minutes perhaps. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about a kilometre. I'm not sure. Not even.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you heard the witnesses describe how they walked up to Pionirska Street. Did you take the same path that they described here in the court?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only path.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And before your encounter with (redacted), did you stop anywhere else on the way from town to Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standing for a longer time? No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is: Did you stop anywhere on the way up to Pionirska Street before you met (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what exactly it was that you said to (redacted) (redacted) and what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I probably hadn't remembered anything had (redacted) (redacted) not been there, but I know him, and I asked him the usual kind of thing. "What's up, Mujo? What -- what -- " And he said, "I'm okay. We have to go to Kladanj." And I know he said that his wife had to go on ahead, had to go earlier. And Mujo said -- he offered two of his cows. He said he -- "I have got two good cows. Do you want them?" And I said, "Mujo, I can't. I haven't got anything to feed the cows with. I can keep them until you return, but I've got nothing to feed them with." So what we chatted about. We discussed things like that. That's what we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. talked about. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for us where precisely it was that you had this conversation with (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road towards the school. Somewhere about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that Prosecution Exhibit 17.3 be placed on the ELMO by the witness. I'm going to ask that he be given a blue pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I'm going to ask you to look at P17.3, and I'm going to ask you whether you can see on that photograph the location where you spoke with (redacted). Please make no mark yet on the diagram. Are you able to see?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask you to put your initials and a circle where it was that you had the conversation with (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And put a circle around it, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And before you give it to the usher, would you please write your name on the bottom of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that it now be placed on the ELMO. And I think it's apparent where you have made the mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would tender that copy of 17.3 into evidence as 17.3.MV to indicate that it was the accused who made these marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P17.3.MV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, (redacted) was a farmer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujo worked in the Terpentin company of Visegrad, but yes, he was a farmer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he had some fields upon which he raised some livestock, including the two cows that he talked to you about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would you say you were better friends with (redacted) or better friends with Meho Dzafic? Who were you closer to?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was closer to Meho Dzafic. I worked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also consider (redacted) a good friend?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were always good friends. He would pass by my house every day on his way to work. We would have a drink very often. Mujo frequented cafes more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mujo wasn't giving you his cows because he didn't want them, he was offering you the cows because he was being forced to leave and he couldn't take them with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that his cows wouldn't perish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he had to abandon his cows; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to leave his house and property.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it seems that on this day, there were two more abandoned animals that fit into the story, yet you were willing to walk all the way up to Vucine on a Serb holiday to care for a horse whose owner you did not know, but you refused to help your good friend take care of the two cows that he had to abandon; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, no. How could I keep two cows? You can't send a cow out in the forest to fend for itself. I would have taken his cows had I had a shed and food to feed them with. Why not? I would give him mine if I had to leave. I would give them to anyone who was willing to look after them and feed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vasiljevic, this is the beginning of the summer. Cows eat grass, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And there was grass in the field of (redacted), was there not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't go and tend to the cows by his house all the time, on his field. If I had my own piece of land and my own shed, I would take them then, but -- like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So as far as you knew, when you refused Mujo's request regarding the two cows, as far as you knew at that time, those two cows would have just perished? You made no arrangements for those cows; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cooperative took the cows and livestock. Generally, the cooperative would do that. They would take the animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you told us a few weeks ago that you may have given Mujo your address and your phone number. Do you recall telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you planned to remain in contact with (redacted); correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would always with Mujo. But unfortunately, he was killed and burnt in the house. We would still be friends today. We never had any disagreements or problems. He was a good man. He liked to have a drink now and again, and I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that you could have done this good friend a great service by perhaps selling his cows and eventually giving him the money; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would I sell them to? I didn't even think about it at the time. I couldn't take them, that was all. I knew that I couldn't take them. Who could I sell his cows to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, when you were up on Pionirska Street talking to Mujo, there were other people there that you recognised; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another man with Mujo. I don't know his name, but he built houses in Sase. Now, whether he had a house up there in Jasarevici, that settlement. The settlement in Sase was called Jasarevici. I know that he was building a house below the road -- under -- below the village. Now, what his name was, I can't quite remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And didn't you also recognise some of the people from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't paying attention to things like that. How would I know? I don't know. What can I tell you about that? I don't know what to say. I know that they came. I know the women came, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, is it your testimony here today that at the time that you were speaking with (redacted), you did not recognise any of the people, other people present, as being from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know the people, but I don't know the names. You showed a picture VG13, when she [sic] testified, but the fat man, but I don't know his name. I know the other one from the cassette, [redacted] [redacted] but I don't know the names. I know the people by sight. I don't know the names, what their names are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair for me to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to check the name that he mentioned on the cassette. Is that a protected witness? The old man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour. The transcript isn't showing the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm thinking the video that you have prepared which includes showing a witness's father going past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That witness is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we'll redact the name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that of the other people around the house, although you did not know their names, you knew them by sight and you knew that they were from the village of Koritnik? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I don't know how many of them I saw. Well, had you asked me exactly, had somebody said -- asked me, "Are they from Koritnik or Osanica?" -- but I know the people, I know them by sight. They're from that area, Zupa. It's all referred to that area, Zupa. I know they're from there, that -- I do know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, you've sat here and you've seen a number of witnesses, both live witnesses and witnesses by videolink, who told us about being present on that day. Perhaps you did not know their name, but would it be fair to say that you did recognise them as they entered the courtroom, as they appeared on the monitor, that you recognised them as people that were present on Pionirska Street on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VG61.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you recognised VG61. Did you recognise VG --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You mean 115?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you recognise VG13 when she entered the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you recognise VG18 when she entered the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe slightly but I could never actually -- had I met her in the street, I would never have known that that was -- I wouldn't know who the person was. Perhaps slightly, but nothing definite.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you recognise VG38?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a child. How old was he, 12, 13? I couldn't recognise him even if I had known him, and I don't know that I had known him ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you recognise VG78?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. They were sisters. No, I wouldn't recognise them either because many years have gone by, how many, nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you heard VG18 describe a brief conversation that she had with you regarding a relative of hers who worked for the same company as you. Do you recall having that conversation with her?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps we talked, but I really can't say. I think she said [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you not to talk about the nature of the relationship or mention that person's name. Was the information that she disclosed here in court regarding that person, regarding where he worked at the time, was that information accurate?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the person is the one I'm thinking of then, yes, we worked in the same company, if that was [redacted]. But he's much younger than her. Perhaps I'm wrong. Perhaps I'm wrong, but I think it's just him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you want to rely upon anything here, I think we're going to have to be a little more specific about the person you're referring to and, if necessary, you can do it in private session. But I don't think that you -- that it's fair to assume that you and the witness are speaking about the same thing, same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps I will ask a few questions to see if I can clear it up and if not, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, try that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking about Witness VG18. Do you see her name on the sheet in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall her testifying regarding where a relative of hers worked?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but she didn't say the name. I think it was -- well, you don't want me to say names. That was the only surname, her maiden name, and I think that's what she said, as you said. And [redacted] did work in the company I worked for. We worked together in the same company. I'm sorry, I mentioned the word [redacted] again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us that you would not have recognised her on the street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you knew this information about her relative because she told you that on the 14th of June; is that correct? That's how you know this information.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that relative of hers, yes, I do. If she didn't say the name but I think that's it because he was the only one in the company with that surname, as a waiter, working as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in fact, when you spoke with her regarding this relative, you told her that he worked in another establishment owned by your company, a different one than the particular cafe that you worked in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what she says, but he did work up there at that time, and we worked together too, for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't have a very clear memory of the conversation you had with her on that day, do you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. She says she asked me, maybe she did. Please believe me when I say this. I don't want to say she didn't. I just can't say. If she says we talked about it, then probably we did, but I don't remember. Maybe we did. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you told us on your first day of testimony that you sometimes forget what you've said and what you've done when you're drinking. Is it reasonable for us to conclude that because you were drinking this day, that is why you do not have a clear memory of the conversation you had with VG18? Can we conclude that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can if we talked about it. Well, why should I remember? Maybe the woman did ask me; I don't want to say she didn't. If she mentioned that relative of hers, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it a fact that when you do drink you sometimes forget the things you say and the things you do and this problem has been an increasing one over the years of your drinking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, in fact, you told us that you -- sometimes you are not aware of the things you do and say, and you gave us as an example not being aware of how you got back to your house, whether you walked, whether somebody drove you, and different things like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm very drunk, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, how drunk would you say you were on this day? Would you consider yourself very drunk on this day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not that drunk. Well, when I fell, yes, I mean the horse fell. We fell together. Well, not that drunk as I was then. Perhaps I wouldn't remember anything. Let me tell you, let me explain it to you, I might not have remembered anything, had not (redacted) been there in that group, I might have passed by. What would I have said to those women? Why would I talk to them? Perhaps if somebody asked me something, I would respond and answer, but I knew nothing about this until The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, my question to you is: Given that you were drinking that day, is it possible you said other things to some of the people there that you now do not have a clear memory of saying?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say. Possibly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I talked to someone, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, do you recall telling (redacted) that everything was going to be all right; did you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the exact conversation, what we said while we -- what could I say? He was leaving his house, his property. What could I say to him? What else could I tell him? What could I say to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me see if this refreshes your memory. In your statement of the 16th on page 86, and I will read you a quote from that, "So I told him," referring to Mujo, "So I told him it's going to be all right, and what else could I have told him?" Does that refresh your memory as to whether you told (redacted) on that day that everything was going to be all right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought they would come back, they would find something there. I don't know, sir. What can I tell you? I can't describe to you exactly what we talked about. It was a long time ago. How we talked, now what we actually said, who, what, I felt sorry for him, and not only for him, I was sorry. The poor man was having to leave. He was leaving his home, his plot of land, and we promised to see each other again to say hello. We were good friends. My wife worked in his village. What can I tell you? What can I say to what you're saying? What happened happened. I really don't know anything about it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this will be a good place to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, we concluded the break with me asking you about whether or not you said to (redacted) that everything would be all right. I'm going to ask you -- because the answer to this question is very important, I'm going to ask you to answer my next question with a simple yes or no. Do you remember saying to (redacted) that everything would be all right? Do you remember saying that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, that everything will be all right. Now, I don't know -- I don't really know how to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a yes or no --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- well, yes. If I said it, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, however, that as you sit here today in court, you do not have a very clear memory of you saying that to (redacted) (redacted)? Isn't that the problem that we're having, that you do not have a clear memory, because you were drinking at the time, of what you said to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember everything that was said, but I didn't say anything bad was said to him, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm wondering whether it's fair to add what you said in that last question, it was because he had been drinking at the time. He has said on a number of occasions that he had not found out about any of this until he arrived at The Hague. Now, if you want to put it to him he is having trouble remembering, fair enough, but to add that it's as a result of that, I'm not sure that he really has accepted that because of the number of times he's referred to the other fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, is your problem with recalling precisely what you did on the 14th of June, is the problem with the length of time that has gone by since the 14th of June, 1992, or is it because you were drinking at the time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I think that the principal problem is the time that has gone by, because I just don't know anything about it, about all these things what happened until I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm sorry to interrupt again, but I'm not sure that you got my point. The question is whether he would have remembered anything that happened on the 14th of June if he had had no occasion to recall it. It's a different issue. If you asked me what I was doing on the 14th of June, 1992, I would have absolutely no idea. Whether I spoke to a particular person at a particular time on a particular street, I couldn't tell you. But if at the time something dramatic had happened which would have impressed these things in his mind, it's quite different. As I understand the defendant's answers, he is saying, "Look, I could have spoken to him. I just never was asked to recall anything about it until I arrived here in The Hague." Now, that's not just the passage of time. It's the need to have to recall it, which is important. Now, I don't know whether we accept him or not. That's a matter we have to determine at the end of the trial or whether we think that what he says raises some reasonable doubt about it. But I think it's only fair that if you want to tie him down, it's not just the extent of the period that has passed, it's the fact that nobody had asked him to recall this until he arrived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So if you want to rely upon his answers, may I suggest you put that to him and see how that goes. In the end, we'll have to determine how we approach it in the light of all of the evidence. But I don't think that you're being quite accurate in the way you put it to him at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me try again, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you've heard the Court's comments. Is your problem with remembering because in your mind nothing remarkable happened on that day to make it stand out in your mind? Is that the essence of your problem with remembering precisely what people said and what you may have said that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time and nothing special happened so that it would be impressed in my mind. Had anything happened, had there been any problem or something, then I would have remembered it. Then I would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So there was nothing remarkable. Had there been something remarkable, you would have a clearer memory of what was said to you and what you may have said to other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have remembered what had happened. But there was nothing that I -- that would have -- that stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let's see whether or not some remarkable things happened on this day. This was the last time that you saw your good friend (redacted) (redacted) alive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in fact, we're now talking about the last words that you and this good friend exchanged; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is also the day that you said that you had this terrible accident with the horse that put you in the hospital for over two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-three days, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we also know from your earlier testimony that you do not seem to have any problem recollecting what you said and what you did not say with the man who told you initially about the horse. You remember that quite clearly; is that correct? Mr. Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was off to get the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that was remarkable enough for you to remember with specificity the conversation that you had with Mr. Ristanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, because I broke my leg that day. So there was reason for me to remember it, because I broke my leg that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And yet you've told us that you do not have a clear memory of what you may have said to (redacted), your good friend, the last time you spoke to him; is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know what we talked about. We were together some 15 or 20 minutes so we must have talked about things. I'm sure we talked about more but we -- but it wasn't anything bad that we talked about. Of course, the bad thing is what happened but what can I do about that? It's by the orders of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you seem to recall quite clearly that (redacted) spoke to you about his wife and where she was at that moment, in the town of Kladanj. You seem to recall quite clearly the conversation that you had with him regarding the cows, both what he said to you and you said to him, yet is it your testimony that you do not have a clear memory of saying to him, "You will be all right."

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, what shall I tell you? Maybe I said it will be all right, thinking that he'd be coming back. I can't give you every word, every sentence. I really can't. I guess we talked about other things, but there was no argument or any problem between us. There was nothing like that ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about some of the other things that witnesses have told us you said to them at that time. One of the witnesses said that you asked the people there if they had gotten settled in the Memic house. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. To begin with, I didn't know. They could have settled in any house. No, I didn't know that Memic's house was empty, and truth to tell, I couldn't care less where they would settle, so they could go to that house or to some other house. I had nothing to do with that, so why would it be up to me to tell them what house to go to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Aside from the name of the person who owned the house, is it possible that you said to these people or that you asked these people were they settled in the house that you were standing in front of and they were around? Can you be sure that you did not ask them were they settled in that house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know. It wasn't mine to accommodate people. I don't know. I mean they were around me. They could go to whatever house. I had nothing to do with where those people would be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is evidence before the Chamber that you said, "It's a good place to spend the night." Can you be sure that you did not say that to anybody on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. Why should I? I mean any house is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's also evidence that you said that there was a bus coming the following morning. Can you be sure that you did not say that to any of the people at that house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter any one of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking about in front of the house. The witnesses described you saying this at the front of the house. Can you be sure that you did not tell anyone that day that there would be a bus coming the following day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mujo was saying that they were too late, that there was no bus. What did we talk about? I suppose somebody told them that it would be coming the next day. I don't know, sir. Again, I'm saying I had no bad intentions, and they could go to whatever house they liked. I didn't organise those convoys. I didn't try to watch them or monitor them or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, they are saying that you told them that a bus would be coming the next day, and I'll ask you to answer the question with a simple yes or no. Did you tell those people that a bus was coming the next day; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Somebody else told them. They were saying that somebody had told them that they would be taken away the next day, I don't know, and that they were late. I didn't know that until I saw (redacted) (redacted). I didn't know they would be going. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you said, "I don't think so." Can I take from that that it is possible that you did say that a bus was coming the next day, but you have since forgotten that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my responsibility. How could I know? How can I say it will be -- the bus will be coming? I didn't work for the transport company. How could I say something like that? How could I guarantee that a bus would be coming? I didn't do that. I didn't -- I don't know how to explain it. How can I say anything? How can I guarantee him that the bus will be coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, is it possible you told somebody that day that a bus was coming the next day; yes or no, please? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A witness testified several weeks ago that you told the people that they should stay in that house. Without explaining how and why or what your responsibilities were, can you tell us, yes or no, did you ever tell anyone on that day that they should stay in the house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did, no. No, they could go to whatever house as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, regarding whether or not you wrote something down, you've 13 testified yourself that, "I could have perhaps given him," meaning (redacted) (redacted), "my address or telephone number." Do you recall testifying to that earlier in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So at least on the issue of writing something, you do entertain the possibility that you may have written something down, and you may have given it to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I gave it to him but that I had written for him a guarantee or something like that as they are saying, that is, no. I mean, who am I to issue any guarantees and who is responsible for such things. He knew what I was, I mean, that I was a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if I'm correct, you do not dispute that you may have handed (redacted) a piece of paper that you wrote on. What you do dispute is what was written on that piece of paper; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I couldn't give him any guarantees. If I did something, I could have given him a telephone number or address, nothing else at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to be clear, what was written on that paper was written in the presence of (redacted). It wasn't a piece of paper that was written on earlier in the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave it to him, then I gave it to him then, but I just have no recollection of these papers or anything. I'm not sure about any of this. I don't know. It's all "perhaps."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you refresh my memory? Am I correct in thinking that (redacted) (redacted) lived across the street from you and very close to your home? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not across the street. He lived in Sase. It could be a kilometre and a half from my house towards Banja, towards the Spa. That is, you turn right to go to Sase, about a kilometre and a half. But he would pass going to work every day. I saw him often. I knew him well, and his wife, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
