utterances.text: And you testified that he stopped by your house very frequently. I think maybe even you said every day. Is that correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He passed by every day, yes, going to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that despite that, (redacted) did not know your address? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he didn't know the street. Whether he knew the street -- perhaps he knew the street, but I guess he didn't know the telephone number. If I gave it to him, that is, because I don't remember doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You heard Witness VG84, who was a boy at the time, standing quite close to you when he says you addressed the people there. He said that you stated a number of things to those people. He said that you said, "My name is Mitar Vasiljevic. I represent the Red Cross. I am in charge of your accommodation and security." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't work for the Red Cross, and I could not say that. He was a child, so I can't remember him. But I could not say that, because I did not work for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, we know that you never worked for the Red Cross. The question is: Did you ever represent to people that you worked for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't work for the Red Cross, and I couldn't say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever wear the symbol of the Red Cross on your camouflage uniform during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a camouflage uniform in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever wearing the insignia of the Red Cross on your person?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this red ribbon. Perhaps this is what they thought was the Red Cross emblem. But that I said anything to them like that, no. It never crossed my mind, because I never worked for it. Then I'd have to be there the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We know from your prior testimony that the red ribbon had no words on it and had no symbols on it. It was a simple plain red ribbon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that that is all you wore? You never wore the insignia of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Why? I didn't work for the Red Cross, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us on the last day that we were in session that you had reviewed or read the Defence witness -- statements given by Defence witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence witnesses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And have you read the statement of a Defence witness by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The lawyer read it to me. That is my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And have you read the statement of the Defence witness by the name of Dragisa Lindo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me tell you, I never had them with me, so I can't really remember all I said. I mean, the lawyer read them to me, so that I really didn't have them with me, those witness statements, I mean, in the cell to study them properly, only what the lawyer read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you will recall that both of those men claim that they both, they both saw you with a Red Cross insignia on your uniform? You will recall that, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With that ribbon. I don't know. As I said, I do not have a single witness statement in my cell. I could have, but I never kept them in the cell. So I just don't know. I only know what the lawyer read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are these witnesses mistaken if they say that they saw you wearing a Red Cross insignia? Are they mistaken if they should say that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they saw that ribbon, and what they took it to mean, I don't know. They will explain it when they testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it a fact that even Serbs, even your own neighbours, believed that you were associated with the Red Cross because of things you said or things you wore? Isn't it a fact that even your neighbours believed you were associated with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. Well, he will be testifying. But the Red Cross would have known had I worked for them, because these humanitarian and whatnot, surely they would have known it had I worked for the Red Cross, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us, before we took the two-week break, telling us that (redacted) may have asked you about the red ribbon you were wearing? Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, I suppose he did ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you also remember telling us that, and I quote, "I may have said something"? Do you recall telling us that in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if I said that I was responsible for the cleaning of the town, but I couldn't say that I was responsible for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you -- do you have a clear memory regarding what you said to (redacted) regarding the red ribbon? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I mean, how can I tell you all that I talked with him about? It was a long time ago. How can I know now what he asked me and what I asked him? But there was -- there was nothing bad that we talked about, and I didn't think anything bad about him or that we talked about anything untoward. I don't know. I mean, what happened, happened. What can I do about it? What can I do about it? And I am very sorry that he dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it possible --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I --- I've been accused of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it possible that on that day you were wearing this Red Cross insignia as described in the statements of two Defence witnesses and that that is why some of these witnesses believed that you were representing the Red Cross? Isn't that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that ribbon, I guess they must have thought that this red ribbon was some Red Cross emblem. That's perhaps how they saw it. But how can I say, I mean what people think about something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we leave this area, is it possible that you may have said anything to these people which you can now remember which you believe that they misinterpreted, just as you're telling us that they may have misinterpreted the red ribbon? Can you recall anything that you said that they may have misinterpreted?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I repeat, I cannot recollect every conversation. But I did not say anything bad to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, at some point you had a drink with (redacted) (redacted); is that correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in your testimony, you told us that you had a bottle of brandy with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you had this bottle yourself from earlier in the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did (redacted) have any bottle of any type of alcohol that you could see during the time that you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- no. Perhaps he did, but in a bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did (redacted) ever leave where you were talking with him, go to a store, and buy a bottle of brandy? Did he ever do that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't think so. Perhaps later, I don't know, when I had left. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to read you a portion of your statement given on the 16th of November last year at page 86, and I'm quoting, "And so I said," referring to yourself, "'Shall we have a drink, Mujo?' He said, 'Very well.' Then he went to the store, got a bottle of brandy and so we had some drinks." Do you admit or deny that you said that on the 16th of November?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he said "went," I read that. I didn't express myself properly. You asked me the next day about that and I told you. I was ashamed to tell you then. Now, it's up to you -- I was ashamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ashamed to tell me what?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ashamed to say that I drank so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that is why you told myself and the investigators that it was Mujo that bought the brandy. That is the reason why you told us that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I corrected myself there. I said I went and bought the brandy, something like that. I have it -- there are some mistakes there and it's not quite clear, but to tell you the truth, I was ashamed, but what can I do? And the hospital, neuropsychiatry, and everything -- well, I was ashamed to say that I was carrying a bottle with me and that I was an alcoholic, I was ashamed, although I did own up to it and I did go for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, on the 16th of November, because you were ashamed of your alcoholism, in your statement, you said something which you knew to be false, and that is that (redacted) had bought the brandy. Is that correct, you said something you knew to be false?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. I wouldn't say that I said it. I said, "went bought brandy," I wasn't specific. I don't think I actually said that Mujo went off. Does it say Mujo went to the shop to buy brandy, because I don't think I said it as explicitly as that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll read it to you again. "'Shall we have a drink, Mujo?' He said, 'Very well.' Then he went to the store, got a bottle of brandy, and so we had some drinks." Did you say that on the 16th of November?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation said, "... went to the store and bought a bottle of brandy." It says I went. Now, there's something between the "I went" and "went" and "he went" in the Serbian translation. I don't think -- well, I did say it. Well, I was ashamed to say that I carried the bottle with me, and that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you do admit that you said Mujo went to the store and bought the brandy. You admit that now.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't think that's what the translation -- that's not what I wanted to say, but for me to buy it. It's different to go off and buy the bottle and it's different to carry a bottle with you, and as I said, this -- I was ashamed. And had you not asked me and I was treated for alcoholism, I was in hospital, and probably I wouldn't have mentioned that either had you not actually asked me. So "went," "bought."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, can you ask him those questions and ask him to exclude what was in the Serbian translation and ask him what his memory is now, because it's anything but clear to me from his answer as it's being interpreted to me what it is he is saying. "I was ashamed to say I carried the bottle with me," suggests that he did, in fact, carry the bottle with him but was ashamed to say it and, therefore, ascribed the action of purchasing it to this other fellow. But I'm not sure that is what he's saying in the overall context. If it's important, you better tie him down without reference to what's in the Serbian translation of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, your statement is in evidence and the Court can review that if they wish. Let's forget about the statement for the moment. What is your testimony here today regarding the bottle of brandy? Where did the bottle of brandy come from?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried it, sir. I carried it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also carry the glasses for the brandy?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did those come from?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Mujo must have gone into a house and brought out the glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time you had a drink with Mujo, were there other people in the area?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there probably was, the houses nearby, people pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the people that were around you, were they the people whose names you did not know but whom you recognised from the villages of Sase and Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did you drink with Mujo before you left that place?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, perhaps 20 minutes, perhaps more. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall how many drinks you had?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I left him the bottle. I don't know. I think -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to get to where the horse was supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not far, five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us what time of the day, approximately, do you arrive to where the horse is?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, perhaps half past 4.00, 5.00, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So somewhere between 4.30 and 5.00 in the afternoon, you arrive to the place where the horse is; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Perhaps the time is not exact to the minute or to the half hour, give or take a half hour, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where, precisely, was the horse when you first saw it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vucine, it's a settlement right above Pionirska. There's a shed, a wooden one, and there is a meadow in front of the shed, and he was tied in a plum tree. He was tethered with a long piece of rope.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how was it you knew that this horse was the horse that you were coming to get?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ristanovic explained to me where the house was and everything up there. It's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The meadow that you're referring to, was there a fence around the meadow?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How large was this horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not very big, a smaller horse, smaller horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us when you were standing, or if you were standing next to this horse, how far up on your body would the back of the horse come?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe up to here, like this. I don't know. But it was a smaller horse anyway, not big.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you were indicating the top of your chest by your collarbone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Collarbone, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He's saying on the -- on his chest, what would normally be regarded as his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you happy with that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, had you ever seen this horse before?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know anything about this horse prior to this day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a saddle on the horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the horse have shoes on its hooves?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the horse have a bridle in its mouth?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not what goes into the mouth. We call that a uzda, the metal part. He just had the bit around, without the thing that goes inside the mouth, without that metal bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he just had the piece of harness that surrounded his nose. He had no metal bit in his mouth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you -- you've told us about a shed. Did you go into that shed and look for either a saddle or a bridle with a bit?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would I be correct in saying that a horse that is to be ridden ordinarily would have shoes on its feet, would have a saddle put on it, and would have a bridle with a bit? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably he did have a bridle and saddle, the owner, but I didn't need it. I wasn't intending to keep it for myself. I was going to refuse anyway. But he probably did. But that's not what I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you get up onto this horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how is it that you got up onto this horse without a saddle and without stirrups?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went upwards and took him to a place that was downwards, and I'd ridden horses when I was younger hundreds of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let me see if I understand what you're telling us. You took the horse to a sloped part on the meadow and you were able to mount the horse by standing on a --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- higher part of the meadow? Am I correct in thinking --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking that that would have required you to jump up onto the horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You see, the bank -- embankment was a little raised. I didn't actually have to make any precipitous movement and jump that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you mounted this horse, that you have no personal knowledge whether this horse has been broken for riding or trained for riding, that you mount this unknown horse without a saddle and without a bridle with a bit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an old horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as soon as you were up on this horse, you begin to ride to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you able to control the horse even though it has no bit in its mouth?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could. It was a calm horse. It was a very calm horse. If he was a young -- to tell you the truth, if he was a younger horse, I wouldn't dare, but he was a calm, old horse. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You knew that before you went for the horse or you knew after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time you went up to look for the horse, you did not know the age of the horse or whether it had been trained for riding; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stroked it. And you see, a horse -- well, I wouldn't have dared if it was a young horse, a younger horse. A younger horse, you know, he would have moved around. I wouldn't dare. Even if I had ridden horses before, I wouldn't dare. I would have if he had a bit and bridle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the area where the horse was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Reins." Sorry, not "bit," "reins." Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The area where the horse -- you found the horse, would it be fair for me to say that it was a very rural area with many meadows and many hillsides?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are lots of houses up there. There are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Houses belonging to only Muslims or Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up there? Well, I don't know what villages. I think they're Muslim. Vucine are mostly Muslims. Now, which those villages were, I think they were Muslim. I'm not sure, because they're tied to Dobrun further on up. I'm sure there are Serb houses, too, but the majority are Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that with respect to grass for the horse to graze on, there was substantially more grazing area for the horse in Vucine than on the abandoned railroad tracks where you brought the horse? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I wanted to take him up to Drinsko, the Serbian village, if somebody would take him. But nobody would take him up there in Pionirska. And up there they were Muslim villages, so I rode him. I liked -- I liked to ride. Like a -- as a -- when I was a child, I fell lots of time. I had to go to hospital once or twice falling off a horse before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree that with respect to the amount of food or grass available for the horse, that there was more grazing land where the horse was as opposed to where you let the horse go? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is grass up there, enough. All over. There was grass all over the place. It was summertime. Yes, there was grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you let the horse go by the railroad tracks, how did you know that the horse would go to this village of Drinsko rather than simply go home?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood correctly, and I think that the English text reads that way, the question was translated as saying that Mr. Vasiljevic let the horse go. But he fell with that horse. He didn't let him go anywhere. So I think that question is a leading one for something that was not stated in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's perfectly permissible to ask leading questions in cross-examination. The only problem that I would have with it is that it appears to be put as a version which the witness has already given. I think you'll have to sort that one out, Mr. Groome. That is certainly the way I understood it when the question was asked, and I was thinking of precisely -- myself wondering how he let it go, let the horse go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you told us it was your intention to let the horse go by the railroad tracks so that it would travel down the railroad tracks to the village of Drinsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I intended to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you intended that as you took that horse out of the meadow where you found it grazing by the plum tree; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why was it that you believed if you let this horse go on the railroad tracks that go to Drinsko that the horse was going to follow those railroad tracks to Drinsko instead of simply going back to its home where you took it from?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had to go back through the town, and I don't think the horse would have gone back through town. I think he would have chosen the open space. But he could have gone back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us about all of your experience with horses. Maybe you can tell us, isn't it quite common for a horse, if it gets lost or gets loose, will very often return to a place that it knows, a place that it -- to its home, to where its owners live?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. A horse wants to go back usually, but that's why I was going to take him up on the railroad tracks. I don't know if he would know how to get back. I would take him up there to Duca and he would go to the village, and somebody would take him in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you rode the horseback towards Visegrad, you went back down along Pionirska Street; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long did it take you to ride the horse from where you found it to where you had the drink with (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long did you spend up where the horse -- where you found the horse? How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. Not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: More than five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, ten minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you arrived back at the house on Pionirska Street, where you saw Mujo, approximately 20 minutes after you left?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Do you mean in the house or by the house? I went back by the house. The same -- I went back the same street, the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you would have passed by where you and Mujo had the drink, approximately 20 minutes after you left; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was windy and it was about to rain, that kind of thing. There was a strong wind blowing, and it looked as if it was going to rain. I don't remember seeing Mujo, the people, any more. I was riding the horse until I reached town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you left Mujo the first time, did you -- you knew that you would be coming back in that direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had no other way to take. Perhaps I could have gone roundabout, taken a roundabout route, but that was the only short route, the shortest way of getting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So did you expect to see Mujo again as you passed by?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was -- it was -- there was a storm brewing. It was windy. It was going to rain. They'd probably gone into the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm getting at, Mr. Vasiljevic, is that at the time you left (redacted), was it your intention to stop on your way back, perhaps have another drink from the bottle of brandy which you had given him? Was that your intention at the time you left (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I seen him on the road, I would have stopped. Quite certainly I would have stopped, had I seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did (redacted) give you any indication after you left or that on the 14th, he was going to go somewhere else? Did you believe that he was going to leave where you saw him that day on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They said they would go the next day, that they didn't have a bus that day, didn't have transport. And I told him that I would come to say goodbye, to have another drink, and I would have gone had it -- but I broke my leg, they lost their lives, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that when you passed the house, you could not see any of the people that you saw there before?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember because, as I say, there was a storm brewing. It was very windy, and it was just about to rain. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, as you rode past this house where you saw these people, you did look to see if you could see them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Had Mujo been on the road, I would have got down off the horse and had a drink with him. I'm sure I would have done that and stayed for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But not only did you not see Mujo, you did not see anybody by the house at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it possible that you did see people at the house and you now have forgotten?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I did, but I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But your best memory as you sit here today is that you don't recall seeing anybody at the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's how it was. I don't know. I don't think I did. As I say again, it was just about to rain. There was a lot of wind. It was very windy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see any cars or other vehicles in front of the house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know. Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that had you seen some cars or vehicles that you recognised, that you would have remembered it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I seen Milan Lukic's car or him, I would have remembered it. I repeat, I just don't see -- don't remember seeing him that day in town, or I don't know. I don't know. I can't say anything exactly. I had just left from up there and I was moving past. I didn't stop anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as you went past the house, you did not hear anybody either, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember all those men, women. I don't remember anything. I am telling you there was -- it was very stormy. There was a lot of wind. It was about to rain, and it was really a very strong wind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it still -- given the stormy conditions that you are describing, was it still light out at this time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, yes, one could -- yes, there was plenty of light.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want you to think very carefully about this next question I'm going to ask you. You have heard a number of witnesses express their belief that it was you who told Milan Lukic that they were there in that house, that you were the only person who knew they were there. Perhaps it wasn't Milan Lukic who you told. Is it at all possible that you said something to someone about the people at that house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand what you're asking me, that I -- that I told Milan Lukic that they were in that house; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you tell Milan Lukic that they were in that house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was going from Pionirska, and less than five minutes later, riding this horse, I fell off it and broke my leg. I did not see Milan. I could not see him because five or ten minutes after I left Pionirska down to the restaurant, that is where I fell and broke my leg and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you say anything to anybody about the Muslims in that house on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. I couldn't. I returned with the horse, fell off it, broke my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure you never told anyone about the people in that house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure because I didn't have time to say that anything to people, and I had nothing to do with it. I simply had no time to do that because I rode past, and when I reached the grill restaurant, the horse skidded, I fell off, broke my leg. So I simply had no opportunity to tell -- to say anything to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it a fact that as soon as you fell off the horse, some of the first people to come and to give you assistance were White Eagles, and they came from the hotel right where you fell off the horse; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't the Eagles, it is a witness who will be coming here, Pero Mitrovic, a teacher from Visegrad and his colleague, Djordje Miscevic, not the White Eagles. And they put me in a car when the driver came, Zivorad Savic, not the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- a different Defence witness, a witness by the name of Hajro Hadzo. And I'm going to ask you -- yes. And that person's statement, the person says, "From my place I could hear Mitar scream in pain. I saw soldiers from the Eagles unit come out of the Hotel Visegrad trying to help Mitar." Isn't it a fact that members of the White Eagles came to your immediate assistance as you fell off that horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What White Eagles? Well, the witness will be coming. I believe he was on the reserve police force, a teacher from Visegrad. No, no, no. And another one, I mean the other one, he was also a teacher. But yes, they were in the hotel. That is true. Yes, they were in the hotel. That's true. They held the hotel. But not the White Eagles, no, no, no. No, no, no, they were, I think, the police reserve force. They are older than I am. They are serious people. They took me in the car, and the witness will be coming. He knows who was there better than I do because I hurt at the time. What, White Eagles? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone in a uniform of any sort coming to help you when you fell from the horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first one to arrive was Petar Mitrovic and Djordje Miscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the reserve police, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there other people there in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, what shall I say? When I fell, the rain had already started falling so that there weren't many passersby. And of course I hurt terribly. It was excruciating pain and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it possible that you told anybody at that time, after you fell off the horse, that there were Muslims up in the house on Pionirska Street? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Do you know what kind of pain that is? I mean you can't think of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about Mr. Lepenica. Have you read the statement of that witness who will be appearing on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lepenica was a Muslim man who, together with you and several other people, shared a room in Uzice hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you shared this room with Mr. Lepenica and the other people for a number of days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lepenica, in his statement, tells us that you described to him and to the other people in that room just exactly how it was that you came to have this horse or be riding this horse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he will testify, I imagine, that you told him that the horse did not belong to this person up in Vucine, but in fact belonged to an imam or a Muslim holy man and that you killed that imam and stole his horse. Did you ever say that to Mr. Lepenica or any of the other people in that room?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never told him that. And there were two imams in Visegrad, and I suppose -- I would testify about this. There are two hodzas, and I know both of them. They didn't leave -- they didn't live far from me, where I worked. And one Muslim mentioned to me that a hodza had been killed, not that I killed a hodza.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you knew that a Muslim holy man by the name of Hodzic, I believe you said, that he had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hadjji? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is the name of the imam who you found out had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He's not Hadzic. Imam, that is a hodza. A hodza is a religious leader or something like the priest is with the Serbs. Not Hodzic. It was a hodza. "Imam," that is what you call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did that person have a horse?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How could he? I mean, he lived in the town. They had a house that is -- that -- a religious house just below Panos. I know both of them. One was of quite advanced age. The other one was younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you never said to Mr. Lepenica or anyone that you stole the horse after killing an imam?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Somebody would have testified that he had been killed. Imam is a hodza. I think that there were two witnesses who spoke about that. And they are both alive to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after having spent such a long time in the hospital, can you tell us the names of some of the other people who were in that hospital room that you shared with Mr. Lepenica?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see that he says eight, six. Well, he changed rooms, as far as I can see, four times, but he was there, and I, and two Serbs from Uzice, one man quite elderly. I know he had some knee complaint. Lepenica didn't have a leg. And next to Lepenica there was another Serb who had been in a traffic accident, and I think that his leg got septic, so he had to get the metal pins out of his leg because there was a septic condition. But I think that he changed four rooms. I believe that we were -- I mean, people who were bedridden. Other people could move in and out of the room. I just couldn't. I was just bedridden.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of any of the Serbs whom you shared a room with at this point in time when Mr. Lepenica was in the room too?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That elderly man, I think his last name was Jovancevic, but he was of quite advanced age, 70 or more I would say. But the other one, I tried to think about that and I don't know. But one can find it in the hospital records. I believe his surname started with an "L", but I just don't know. He was tall, thin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lepenica, also in his statement, says that on the wall of the room you drew a picture of yourself riding a horse and that in one of your hands you drew the picture of a megaphone. Did you ever draw such a picture on the wall of your room?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, sir, when I tell you that I wouldn't be able to draw a hand. Draw a horse? I wouldn't know how to draw a hen, if you will believe me. To draw a hen properly, I wouldn't have been able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Lepenica, he's not from Visegrad, is he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's from Gorazde. I think he told me that he was born in Sarajevo or something like that. I remember he told me he had a daughter who was married to somebody in Macedonia - I remember that - and that he worked in Gorazde, that he was a cook there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But my point is, Mr. Lepenica would have no way of knowing that on at least one occasion in this time period you had possession of a megaphone and used it, would he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been a joke on the patients' part. It must have been that. He said that I -- he says that I drew a horse. No. I'm not able even to draw a hen. I mean, forget the horse. I never knew how to draw. I wouldn't be able to draw a tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But my question, Mr. Vasiljevic, is that not being from Visegrad, Mr. Lepenica -- it would have been impossible for Mr. Lepenica to know that you, in the past, had used a megaphone? That would have been impossible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that every day, various patients came, those who were in the orthopaedic ward, and there were lots of jokes lying about, all sorts. So somebody -- somebody drew a horse. You know, we're in the hospital. We're trying to cheer ourselves up. Everybody's bored. And they -- some of them could walk around. I couldn't. So he -- what did he say, that I draw it on the wall or on a sheet of paper? I don't know. Was it on the wall or was it on a piece of paper that I drew that horse?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the wall.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't. I couldn't possibly --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I was bedridden. I couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You seem to suggest in your last answer that you may have seen such a picture on the wall in your room, and I ask you, did you see such a picture on the wall in your room that perhaps Mr. Lepenica mistakenly assumed that you had drawn?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a newspaper. I know patients found it, and other patients, and just stuck it on the wall above me. They found perhaps a photograph in the newspaper or something, and they stuck it up, not that I drew it. I wasn't able to do that because my legs were fixed, and I had weights on my legs. I was in extension, and I had those weights on a pulley. I wouldn't have been able to turn and draw it, even if I knew how to draw. I could perhaps have do something like that on a piece of paper had I known - if I knew how to draw perhaps, but not on the wall. Besides, no doctor would allow me to draw on the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, was there a picture of a horse on a wall above you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did, from a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did the person on that horse have a megaphone?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, perhaps -- well, people kept bringing me newspapers and pictures, especially there would be a colour photograph with a horse. You know, patients will always be patients. They're trying to make jokes. What do you do in the hospital when the doctors have done their rounds and we're all there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified that you broke your left leg, the lower portion of your left leg, on two occasions, once in 1992 and once in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in 1992, you broke both the large bone and the small bone in your left leg; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure that you broke both bones in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both. Yes, I am sure, hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you so sure because the doctors that treated you told you that you broke both bones in that leg?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hundred per cent sure. But let me also tell you, I think - I don't know - if you break only one bone, then you do not need any extension for your leg. It is to strengthen your muscles because -- because the muscles will atrophy. And that is why you have to put those weights. Because the second time I broke it, it was only the big bone, and they did not apply any weights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In 1993, you only broke one bone, the large bone in your left leg; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's clear, the lower part of your left leg; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you absolutely sure in 1993 that you only broke the large bone on that leg?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why are you so sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctor told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that for at least a period of time, you had possession of all of the X-rays that were taken of your leg, and I believe you explained that somehow they have now become misplaced or lost; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had all these X-rays of the check-ups and the operation, and they were all rolled up like this in a yellow paper. I remember it well. I must have had some 15 X-rays from the check-ups and from the health centres, and I don't know where they are. There were 15 of them. I'm terribly sorry, but I must have -- when I moved house, we threw away a lot of things. And I showed this X-ray when a doctor testified here, and that was the only one I had. I must have had 15 of them, both of my spine. I had at least 10 to 15 X-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of this trial, although none of us here are experts in this matter, we've all looked at the X-rays taken of your leg and drawn certain conclusions. When you looked at the X-ray of your leg in 1992, the ones that you had in your possession, were you able to see the large bone in your leg broken?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it on the X-ray. Yes, you can see both, both these bones, the small one and the large one. You can see it well on the X-ray.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you see, was it clear to you on that X-ray from 1992, could you see the small bone broken on the X-ray that you had?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, sure, because the doctor showed it to me. He showed it to me and explained it all to me. I was told that I was -- that I had more than two bones broken, but you know the leg works because it could turn. In 1992, it could do like this, it could do like this, not in 1993. You could turn it this way and that way as you liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the record, you're making a twisting motion with your hands to describe what happened in 1992, I believe; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I want to be clear about is that at some point, the doctor showed you the X-ray of your leg in 1992 and to you, it was very clear that both the large bone and the small bone had been broken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, similarly, in 1993, did the doctor also show you a copy of your X-ray at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 when I arrived in the hospital, yes, he did this X-ray and I said to the doctor, "Will I again have to have those weights," and he said, "No, because it is a large bone that you broke this time, so we'll apply plaster cast, and that will be it," and I somehow found it easier. "How long will I have to stay in the cast?" "Three months," and so it was three months. And in 1992, I spent three weeks in extension and then had a plaster cast -- for 21 days in extension, and then for two months in plaster cast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did the doctor show you the 1993 X-ray at the time you broke your leg; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you able to clearly see that the large bone in your lower left leg was broken? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. Well, that's how he holds this X-ray to show me, yes, and they all look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you also able to see that the bone, the small bone in your lower left leg was not broken; were you able to see that it was not broken?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't. It wasn't. You can see that. You can see when a bone splits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before you left the hospital in 1992, I believe you left around the 10th or 11th of August, according to your testimony? No, I'm sorry, I withdraw that question. When did you leave the hospital, according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean completely when I was discharged from Uzice, when I left the neurosurgery then?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th July. That's what it says. I spent a long time there, from the 14th of June until the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it true on the very last day that you left, or the day that you left, you attempted to get into the room of Mr. Lepenica and to assault him; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last day? Why, no, my wife had come, and my uncle. I never went up there. My wife and uncle had come to the ward, and they are not adjacent. The orthopaedic surgery is in one building, and the neurosurgery is in a different building. So I had no need to go there. I don't know what he says. I don't know. He was in Gorazde, and I thought up other stories too, but I didn't go to the orthopaedic ward. I was in neurosurgery, and of course I knew when I had to report to the doctor for a check-up, and then -- so that is when I went to Uzice when I had to be -- when I had to have these examinations, follow-up examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you able to give us any idea, Mr. Groome, of how much more time you will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm definitely in the home stretch, Your Honour, and I think it will be perhaps 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So the next witness should be ready after lunch. That's the purpose of my inquiry, We're not complaining. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to go back for just a minute and ask you a few more questions about your criminal record. You've told us about your conviction and incarceration in 1973. By my calculation, that would have been at the same time that you told us you were in military service, and so the question I have for you is: Were you in the military at the time that you engaged in the conduct that subsequently landed you in gaol?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. In 1973, I was convicted by the misdemeanours judge, and in 1973 in November, I was to go to the army. The public prosecutor filed proceedings further, and at the end of 1973, I went to the army. In 1974, I returned from the army to the trial, and once I had completed my military service on the 5th of January, once I came back from the army, I went to complete the three-term -- three-month sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All right. Now -- thank you. Now, when Mr. Domazet asked you about your criminal record, you told us that this was the only time you had been in prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was -- aside from being in prison, was there ever any other time that you were convicted of a crime and perhaps received another sentence such as parole -- probation or a fine?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probation, a conditional sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was -- or excuse me. Can you tell us, were you convicted of a crime then in addition to the crime that you were convicted of in 1973?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a crime. I don't know what year I was put on probation. A man, a neighbour, provoked and insulted my sister. And I mentioned him. We didn't find a common tongue, and I hit him. I don't know what year that was. Was it 1980? Maybe thereabouts. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As you know, we requested and received from the Ministry of Justice in Banja Luka a report of your criminal history, and that is now in evidence as P69 and P69.1 for the B/C/S version. I'm going to read you a paragraph from that, and I ask you, is this the crime or is this the event that you are now referring to? I'm quoting: "Sentence of the Municipal Court, Visegrad, number K23/83, dated the 18th of June, 1983, sentenced to four months of imprisonment, one year on parole, because he committed a crime defined in the Article 53, paragraph 2, and Article 55, paragraph 1 of the penal law of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And I'll read you paragraph 55 or Article 55, paragraph 1 so that you know what exactly is contained in this. "If a person imperils the security of persons by a serious threat to attack upon life or limb of the persons in question or if in that way he causes anxiety among citizens, he shall be punished by imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years." Is that the event that you are talking about on -- a conviction of the 18th of June, 1983?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not like that. It wasn't sent properly. Four months of prison and one year on probation. That is what it was. It wasn't like you said, one year parole or whatever you said. Four months of prison sentence and one year on probation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet. I was waiting for your client to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation] In the translation, I heard "four years and one month," whereas when I read it from the screen, it said the other way round, "four months and one year." So I'm not sure that the accused understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the translation which somehow was delayed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is it you said, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Four months' imprisonment and one year on parole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the dispute then, Mr. Domazet. Your client says it's the other way around, but Mr. Groome is suggesting it is the way he put it. It's a matter which your client can deal with, and if necessary, you can produce the document, one or the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand your problem, but I think that we're now clear. You proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the event that you are describing? It sounds like an altercation between yourself and someone else.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the other person, was the other person convicted of any crime?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was convicted, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his sentence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in courts all the time. I don't know. I mean, for the same, yes, for the same crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his nationality?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was there another time in 1983, during the same month, in June, that you were also before the Municipal Court in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would never have remembered it, but the lawyer brought me a cheque which wasn't covered. I thought that I had not taken some books, perhaps, that I had forgotten to take some books, but the issuance of a cheque without something to cover it. I remember him saying that. I think that I had picked up my salary before my company had actually paid it into the bank. This happened from time to time, and I received a fine. It wasn't a big sentence, a big fine, but it happened very frequently to everyone. We would pick up our salaries on the basis of a cheque before our company had paid in the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so you were -- in all, you've been convicted of three crimes in your lifetime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before the break, I was asking you a few questions about your interaction with [redacted] in the hospital. During the course of your stay there, did you ever make [redacted] sing Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't force him to do that. He's saying these things now. He was in hospital three months. Now, what he -- who he talked about this to, what he did, I don't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you've read his statement and you see that he says that you forced him. Did you ever force him to sing songs by way of threat? If you were confined to your bed and were unable to physically force him, did you ever make a threat to him in order to get him to sing Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't do that, and I think that [redacted] [redacted], and if he heard that I had set fire to one house and another house as -- well, he could say anything. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He also says in his statement that you called him a derogatory term that Serbs use for Muslims around this time period, and that is "balija." Did you call him a balija while you were in the room with him in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can say what he likes. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't. No, why would I say that? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He also says that despite having his leg recently amputated, a reason for him also being in the hospital, that you also forced him to clean the toilet in the room, sometimes several times a day. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't even have a toilet in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a toilet nearby that the patients in your room would use?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was out in the corridor, but our room didn't have a toilet. I didn't use it either, because I was bedridden with the weights on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the doctor wrote. I don't know. On that day, that particular day -- oh, I don't know. How can I explain this to you? I was quite distraught. My nerves were not good. I wasn't feeling well, and they had to tie me up when they took me to the neuropsychological, psychiatric ward. Somebody pushed me, a woman. I was on with -- walking with crutches. She said that I had told her something. I don't know what was the matter with me. I felt afraid. I wasn't feeling well. I was just not myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that one of the reasons you were restrained was because of your violent behaviour in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made a lot of noise, to tell you the truth, to be quite frank. I don't have to hide anything. I shouted a lot. I didn't want to go home. And when I saw a wound and -- I thought that it was death. If I would see a pigeon, I thought that my luck had turned. I hadn't got the feeling that I was able to get hold of myself, to stabilise myself, if I can put it that way. I just couldn't get a grip on myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, did you have any physical altercation with [redacted] during the time you were in Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't say that, but doctor wrote something down. I don't know. I must have said something bad or -- I don't know. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can't -- what can I say? I was completely -- I wasn't good, as far as I remember. I know that they took me away to the neuropsychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [redacted] says that during the stay in the hospital, that you used to brag to him and to the other sick people in the room about the number of Muslims that you killed on the bridge over the Drina. He said that you claimed to have killed them by hitting them with a wooden board in the head and that some of them had jumped into the river before you had an opportunity to strike them in the head. Did you ever say that or anything like that to [redacted] or any of the other people in your room? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And had that happened, somebody would have come to testify that I hit somebody with a board. Somebody would come to testify, somebody who is alive. How do I know what he heard from the other patients? What I want to tell you is this: Perhaps the Serb -- other Serb patients were not -- their conduct wasn't proper perhaps towards him. I don't want to say. There were other Muslims in other rooms. So perhaps -- he was in hospital for three months, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, mister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Yes, Mr. Domazet. I have asked you, Mr. Domazet, please say something that you are objecting --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- because I can't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- both sides of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that by mentioning the name of this witness, we have not made a mistake perhaps. I place the witness on the list of Defence witnesses, although it was a witness whom the Prosecution and the investigators of the OTP took statements that Mr. Groome is bringing up now. He was VG113. That was the number ascribed to him. And with that witness, except for that statement, I have not had any contact, and I do not know whether he wishes to have protective measures; that is to say that his name should not be mentioned in view of the fact that he lives on the territory of the Bosnia Federation. I'm afraid if we mention his full name and if this is broadcast in the media, it might do a lot of harm, and the witness might not want to testify, or that this is publicised can make problems for him. So that I think that it would be better to have used the number that was assigned to the witness. And as far as I remember, it was VG113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, I haven't got the full list in front of me but that's one of your numbers, 113. Had you got -- sorry. You sought an order or had you obtained an order that he be referred to by that pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. All of that -- maybe to clarify, all of the witnesses that the Prosecutor speaks to are assigned VG numbers for Visegrad. Only a portion of those that we sought protective measures for, rather to keep matters simple, we asked that their VG number also be used as their pseudonym to prevent another name for the witness. So although he does have a VG number, we have never sought protective measures for him, and I am unaware of any need that he has for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Except for this: that the situation in which he comes to be a witness for the Defence is just a little unusual. You very properly gave the Defence a copy of his statement. So nobody has had the opportunity of speaking to him as to whether he needs them. What Mr. Domazet says, and I think there is something to it, that publicity being given to his name may frighten him off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no objection if we referred to him by pseudonym. I would not oppose that. I wonder is it possible to go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- on what we've done today and redact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can certainly go back half an hour. Well, within reason. Half an hour might be a little difficult, but we can certainly go back as far as we can and redact what has already been said. But I do think there is something to what Mr. Domazet says from the point of view of perhaps casting some doubt upon his willingness to come along here to give evidence on Mr. Vasiljevic's behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no objection to using a pseudonym. I do not have an independent memory that VG113 is his number. If Mr. Domazet can tell us he's sure of that, then perhaps we will -- we can use that number, or perhaps we can call him "Mr. L" or some other pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure he would appear on anything that the Prosecution has tendered to the Court because we never intended to call him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was looking for a complete list of the pseudonyms. He would not be on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not on ours, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take him as VG200.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, if you can answer yes or no - perhaps you have already - refresh my memory, did you ever say anything to him regarding you killing people on the Drina bridge?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never killed anyone, and especially with a board. What board?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he heard from whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, VG200 also says that you talked, while in the hospital, about your cleaning crew and how your cleaning crew was made up of mostly elderly people. Did you discuss or did you ever talk about your cleaning crew in the presence of Mr. VG200 in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose I did, yes. I must have talked about the cleaning of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Mr. VG200 says that on one occasion, a woman came to visit you, and she informed you that 12 of the people who cleaned under you were so exhausted and frail and that they could not stand any more, and VG200 says you told her that these 12 people should be thrown into the river. Did you ever say that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a concoction. No woman came to see me. What woman would come to see me? No. No, no. Frail? That is that they lost all their strength and everything in about 15 days? No. That's not true. I mean, that is something he heard about me in Gorazde or whatever and then he talked. He couldn't do that, nor could a woman tell me that. What woman?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, Witness VG200 also says that you had a good number of visitors, primarily on Sundays. Did you have visitors while you were in Uzice hospital, aside from your immediate family?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had visitors because I have very many relations in Uzice, and friends. So yes, they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also have visitors that were military personnel? VG200 says that he saw military personnel visit you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military personnel, not a single one. Now, let me tell you, from Visegrad, I know that the president, that is the manager of the firm, Mirkovic, came to see me and brought me some cigarettes, or perhaps a soldier in a uniform came, but some officer to visit me, no. And I don't have any relative of mine who is an officer. As far as I can remember, I don't think there is a single officer in my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Accepting that a military officer didn't come to see you, you have just said that soldiers did come and see, is that correct, that soldiers did come and visit you in Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only me, there were many patients from Visegrad. How do I know? I mean when somebody comes, he simply visits all day with all the patients in the room and how can he know that officers came to see me when they were military soldiers, that is, from -- every day from Roje, from Visegrad, from all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG200 also states that members of the White Eagles came and interrogated him at his bedside. Were you present in the room when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it. I -- I'm not aware that anyone interrogated him. I know that from the Red Cross, a woman came to see with him where he would go after he left the hospital, and I think he was suggesting he should go to Macedonia because his daughter was there, as far as I can remember, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to Exhibit D22; you have it in front of you. Did any of the people that you have listed on D22, did any of them come and visit you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean one person, or any one of them, or what did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Any one of the people that you put on your list, did any of these people come and visit you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay at the neuropsychiatric ward, person 17 and person 10 came for about 10 or 15 minutes. I don't know. I don't remember seeing those others in the hospital ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic ever come and visit you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Never. He never came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about one of the Defence witnesses, Dragan Dikic; what kind of work does he do?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dikic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragisa Dikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dragisa Dikic. What kind of work does he do?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is my neighbour. He is a car mechanic, car mechanic, and does metal repairs, repairs cars, metal, bodywork of the cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that he would repair damage to cars that had been in an accident?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, he still does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
