utterances.text: Now, a search of our records has revealed a claim by a witness that Mitar Knezevic, Dragisa Dikic and yourself committed crimes in and around the town of Visegrad. Did you ever commit crimes in the presence of Mitar Knezevic and Dragisa Dikic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions regarding your treatment after you went to the neuropsychiatric ward. When you were on that ward, did you meet with doctors and discuss some of the concerns and fears that you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I did talk with the doctors. In the early days, they gave me very powerful doses so that I slept all the time, but they asked me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you discuss with them how you felt after your cousin had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not -- I don't really think that I talked with them about that. In the beginning, I think I didn't have -- I didn't even communicate with them. But later on, and at the hospital, they will have those what -- what do you call it -- they have some kind of lessons of classes with patients or rather offer advice. There is some counselling sessions, but that came later when I felt better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In these counselling sessions, did you discuss with them some of the things that were bothering you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, of course. They talk with each one of us and then give you some advice, and there is a psychologist who does that, or they give us some tasks which we are expected to perform to show whether you can do it, whether you're up to it to be -- for instance, in a room, to see whether you can tend to other patients who are in a worse shape than you are, to see if you can help them. I don't know. They have all kinds of services.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you discuss with anybody, with any of the doctors in these counselling sessions, your feelings regarding what occurred at the Drina River on the 7th of June; did you tell them about that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During these sessions, did you see the doctors, would they take notes in your medical file? Did you see them writing notes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they always -- yes, keep up with you and they allow every patient to tell something, to tell a story on something, and then they listen to it. And I suppose, yes, they do take notes because that is -- it is on the basis of that that they prescribe you the medication or further therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it true that when you were released from the orthopaedic ward, you, yourself, did not want to go home, that you, yourself, wanted to go to the neuropsychiatric ward; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is when I was at the orthopaedic ward -- in the orthopaedic ward that I didn't want to go home. But truth to tell, I would have stayed in the hospital, because right across me in another bed opposite me, a patient died. He was an alcoholic too, and he was barely 40. I was very afraid when I saw that. I mean -- and then the doctor said, "Well, see what brandy does to a man." They fought for his life for an hour, perhaps two, and could not help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've referred to yourself several times during the course of your testimony as having been mentally broken at this time, and I'm asking you: Is it only the result of alcoholism or was it also the result of some of the horrible things that were happening during the conflict that you felt mentally broken?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think everything, everything, fear, concern for the children, and all those sorts of problems and alcohol. I was afraid of war. I was afraid of fame, and I was afraid for my children. You don't hear any good news, and it all added up to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that part of your emotional state at this time was not only due to your fears for your own children, but some of the acts that you had witnessed being committed against other people, including Muslims, in the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of it. You simply hear nothing good. At that time, we absolutely heard no good news.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I just have a few more questions for you, then I will be finished. We've now spent the better part of four days listening to your account of these matters which are now before the Court, and I want you to think very carefully before you answer my following questions. The Court will weigh carefully what you have said here during this trial as well as the other witnesses who have appeared before us, and clearly your version is very different than theirs. We have now come to your final opportunity to be completely honest with the Court, if you haven't been so far, regarding the role you played on the 7th and the 14th. I want to put the following facts before you and ask you whether you admit or you deny them. Isn't it a fact that during the summer of 1992, up until the time that you went into the hospital, that at least on several occasions, you associated with and participated with Milan Lukic and his men in the commission of crimes against some of the Muslims living in Visegrad? Isn't that true, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with him only when he committed the crime next to the river, and I said when I was coming from Prelovo in the village of Rusici in the house of the Witness L59's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, Mr. Vasiljevic, that a number of things happened to you around that time that gave you the motivation and the desire to commit crimes with Milan Lukic against Muslims; among those being the death of your cousin at the hands of Muslims, among them your being sent to the front battle line in Rujiste where you felt in danger; among them being the arrest of your "kum," Sredoje Lukic, his being held as hostage, and his dismissal from the police force; and finally among them your being forced to clean the streets in Visegrad with Muslims in punishment for what your -- your failure to complete your duty in Prelovo. Isn't it a fact that all of those contributed to your motivation to work with Milan Lukic to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never committed any crimes with him. As for the 14th, I had no idea what he would do or that he did that. I didn't know it until I arrived in The Hague. And Sredoje Lukic was arrested in mid-April. So why should I take revenge for his arrest? And what else did you ask me about? That relative. Why do I take it out on anyone for my cousin who had nothing to do with it? He was killed on the ground, in the woods. Neither his father nor anybody knows how he was -- who killed him because that was in the woods. Nor did my uncle ask around. I mean, people -- he got killed in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vasiljevic, you would have us believe that during this period of time, you had no feelings of malice towards the Muslim population in Visegrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you like this: I could not set fire to a house, to the smallest one, because I know what trouble -- how difficult it is to build one. And the rest of it, I hope I shall prove. I could not do it to a building because I know what it is to build a house. I had a very hard time building my own, and I haven't finished it yet, and I've been building it for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How would you characterise your feelings towards the Muslim population of Visegrad in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived well with Muslims, with my colleagues. I never had any problem with them. We always worked together. We'd have a drink together. After hours, we'd go to Rogatica, to Uzice whenever -- asked whether you're a Serb, you're a Muslim, we always got on very well. More than 70 per cent of people who will be coming to testify for me are people that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, can you give us one concrete example of during this time of turmoil in Visegrad when Muslims were being taken from their homes and killed and others were being forcibly deported and others were fleeing out of fear, can you give us one concrete example of something you did to help these Muslims who you claim you always had good relationships with?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's addition: In the previous answer, the witness also said that these witnesses were not his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you -- perhaps they are listening to this, but as a matter, when the war broke out and when VG10 and others were captured, one named Dragovic and another, Maric, they were young men, young Muslims, and the Serb police had caught them with weapons, and they -- I let them out on the sly. And they are still alive. I was the one who let them out. When they crossed the hill -- we stayed down there. But when they crossed the hill, I let them go. And I was criticised. Well, not criticised. Why would I do that? But I was the one who let them go, but maybe they're listening to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I testify about this. I'm sorry. Had I meant anything, anything, had I had any ill-intentions, were would I have done that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, the interpreters have given us a note, and in the hurry with which they had to do it, perhaps it's not very clear, but you can see just coming up to the top of the screen now, the witness's answer: "I lived well with Muslims, with my colleagues. I never had any problem with them." Do you see that answer there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the interpreters note, just after your question and before the answer is: In the previous answer, the witness said these are also not his colleagues. Now whether that means there was contradiction in the answer or whether they're correcting that answer saying "not colleagues," I'm not sure, but I think we better have it made clear. Perhaps you might like to ask the witness what it was he intended to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, can you clear up what it is you are -- clear up the Court's concern? Were the people that you were referring to your colleagues or were they not, these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry. I'll read you -- it's disappeared from the screen now. I'll read you what he said. The question was:

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You would have us believe that during this period of time, you had no feelings of malice towards the Muslim population in Visegrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you like this: I could not set fire to a house ... et cetera. And he goes on to deny the facts. Then the question:

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How would you characterise your feelings toward the Muslim population of Visegrad in June of 1992? The answer is recorded in these terms:

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived well with Muslims, with my colleagues. I never had any problems with them. We always worked together. We'd have a drink together. And then he went on to talk about going to have a drink with them. Now, it's that which the interpreters have come back with a note saying in the previous answer, the last I read, the witness said that these were also not his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreter believes that he meant witnesses testifying in his favour, that those were the people he did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. I think that's made it clear. I'm sorry to have done that, but when we came back to it, bearing in mind this is quite an issue you're raising with him, I wanted to have it very clear on the transcript. So he's talking about the witnesses, not his colleagues that he worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it true that during the times that you were present with Milan Lukic, you came to learn that Milan Lukic most often told his intended victims lies to get them to remain calm, to help him commit the crimes against them? Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that during the times that you were with Milan Lukic and his group, you came to learn that one of the weapons that they used against their victims was to tell them lies, lies to get them to remain calm, lies to make it easier for them to commit crimes against them? You, yourself, have given us several examples of this. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at Sase, next -- by the river, it's true that he lied about the exchange and all that. But what do I know what devices he resorted to? I mean, witnesses described me on Pionirska, something, but I wasn't all that much with him. I was his kum. How he deceived those people when I went to the hospital, I suppose he tried to deceive them in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And even in the village of Musici, didn't you come to learn that he told those people to remain in the village, that they would be safe there? Wasn't that another lie that Milan Lukic told the people to assist in committing a crime against them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did nothing that day. I mean, harass anyone or took money from anyone or beat anyone. He didn't. He really didn't. Now, after a few days, I could see that he had been there and taken girls to rape them and (redacted), or - I don't know - plunder, that he took people away and kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were present on the first day, on the first day when he gathered the people of Musici and instructed them to remain in the village, and he assured them that they would be safe in that village? You were present that time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked for weapons, who had any weapons to return them over. Listen, I mean, that's Milan -- that was Milan's doing. But he was cunning, he was clever. He would never tell anyone who'd do that. I mean, that's the kind of man he is. I don't know while he was there and then while he was hiding. I don't think anyone knew where he was hiding. Perhaps there was somebody, somebody who was close to him. But I don't think -- even if he told you where he was hiding, I don't think you should believe his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's very clever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- isn't it a fact that during the times that you committed crimes with Milan Lukic, you also told the victims lies in order to keep them calm, to help Milan Lukic commit these crimes? One of the examples, one that you've told us is to the people of Musici when you told them it would be all right. Isn't it a fact that you also told lies to the victims of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I did not know that he would come back the next day or the day after that. That day he didn't do anything, and Milan wouldn't have never told me that he would be going there tomorrow and doing that. I had no hand in it. I could not send him anywhere or stop him from doing something, because the authorities did not stop him. And I most certainly could not do it. Milan is that kind of man. If I were a member of his -- a member of his, he would have invited me to come to Musici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it true that on the 7th of June, 1992, anything that you may have said to Meho Tesovic before his death to comfort him was simply a trick to ensure that he was calm and to make it easier for you, Milan Lukic, and the other two men to escort him down to the river and to shoot him and the six other men in the back? Isn't that in truth what happened on the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. On the life of my children, I did not know that he would kill them. How did I know that he was arresting them and that he would do that? He did not need me. He planned that. He decided that. I didn't. I didn't. I couldn't kill my colleague, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it a fact that on that day at the river bank, you were in fact in possession of an automatic rifle, and you did point it at those fearful, begging men, those unarmed men lined up along the river bank, and you fired into the backs of their heads and into their backs in an attempt to kill all of them? Isn't that in fact what really happened?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th, I never had a weapon. After I left the prison, never. One witness said a semi-automatic rifle and another witness said automatic rifle. Well, there's a big difference between the two. But I didn't have it. And even had I had one, I wouldn't have fired it, because I knew that I had turned over my weapon - I know that - at Bikovac, at the command. And even had I had a weapon, I wouldn't have dared before God, because these are people that I had worked for a long time with, and he taught me things. He did not deserve that. He was my elder colleague. We worked together for years. And it's not all that easy to kill a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it a fact that your poor mental state was in fact the result of your guilt, the images of the crime that you had participated in on that day, the 7th of June? Wasn't that a contributing factor to your poor mental state?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was difficult for me then. It's difficult for me now, especially when I stand accused. But I had absolutely no idea that Milan would bring those people. I had no idea what he was going to do. He had planned it all. He did it all on his own, of his own back. What am I to him? He could have brought other people, and he did. I don't know what all else he did. He could -- I know somebody said that he cut off somebody's head and paraded it around the school. Sir, I was -- I couldn't -- I was so small in comparison to him. He didn't need me for anything. What would he need me for?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, on the 14th of June, isn't the truth of what happened that day that after you convinced these people to remain in the house, assured them that they would be safe, just as Milan Lukic had done to the people of Musici, that after you had done the first part of the crime, setting up the crime, that you went directly and immediately from that house not to save some lost horse but to let Milan Lukic know that you now had more Muslim victims on which -- upon which crimes could be committed, crimes such as the crime you participated in on the 7th of June? Isn't that in fact what happened? You went directly to Milan Lukic and told him about the people you had convinced to stay in that house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you that I went to fetch the horse. I couldn't see him. And Milan Lukic, he knows it better than I do, where they are. So after 3.00, when they came to loot them, eight to ten, as the witnesses stated, am I the only person who knew where those people were? It's a street. First of all, I was drinking, and Milan wouldn't believe anything I said. He didn't drink. He didn't smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, on the 14th of June, not only did you tell Milan Lukic about these people, isn't it a fact that you returned to the house with him and you remained outside that house while Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Susnjar were inside robbing these people of their last few possessions? Isn't that in fact what occurred on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in front of that house, never, never, and never, nor did I know that they were robbing, never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- didn't you, in fact, as witnesses have testified here, assist Milan Lukic and the other men in moving people out from the house by the road and to the house at the back in order to kill them? Isn't that in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was 11.00, half past twelve. I was in Uzice, in the hospital. I couldn't have been present physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it true that you did not break your leg falling from a horse but that you broke your leg on the steep and slippery bank of the creek by the house that was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know if I've understood you, that you -- you say that I broke the leg by the house that was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking you, isn't it a fact, isn't the truth that you broke your leg slipping during the commission of the crime against those people when you went around the back of house and you fell on the steep and slippery bank of the creek?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a pure fabrication, sir. I have witnesses. They know where I broke my leg. I have witnesses. There are doctors in Visegrad when I was admitted. And this was happening at 11.00, half past eleven at night. It is a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't the truth of this case that the crime did not begin when the match was struck at the rear of that house? It did not even begin at the time that you convinced these people to remain in the house, that perhaps the first act in furtherance of this crime was your presence in Pionirska Street earlier in the day, trying to convince Muslims who may have been hiding in their homes to come out and identify themselves? Isn't that in fact when this crime began?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have nothing to do with that. I don't know. On the lives of my children I say this: that Milan would do that and that and what he was going to do. That I agreed, of course I did not agree. Had I not broken my leg, I would have told you everything otherwise, whether 1 or 50 of them were present, but I can't say -- I can't tell you anything about that. I can't tell you anything about the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Court. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, Mr. Groome questioned you at length about what the notion of kum and kumship represents in the Serbian -- with the Serbian people, and in your particular case, the kumship relations between the Lukic family and the Vasiljevic family. But you answered in detail and said who could be eligible for a kum and how you came to be chosen to be the kum at the wedding ceremony of Milan and who christened his children. Now, if you remember, you said that it could have been -- asked by Mr. Groome, you said that it could have been four members of the family, you or your brother or the children of your brother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me, my brother, and my uncle's sons; that is to say, the children -- yes, my uncle's sons. And let me tell you that I am the eldest of the four of us. So by order of seniority, I was to be kum, although it needn't be like that every time. But I was the oldest, so it would be on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's what I was precisely asking you. Is your brother a younger brother? Your brother, he's younger?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's nine years younger than me, my brother is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you said that custom has it that you usually follow the order of seniority. From your father it goes down -- it is passed on to the next oldest child, which was you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So when you answered Mr. Groome's question about that, you said, "My brother lived in Belgrade and I lived in Visegrad." So that wasn't the only reason, I assume, but the reason you have just explained to us.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be -- I would be the one chosen because of my seniority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we are talking about Milan Lukic's marriage, do you remember that day well?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was a marriage ceremony? A civil service, was it, or in the church? Did it take place in the municipality or in the church?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality, before a registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is customary that in marriages of that sort, in addition to the bride and groom there are two kums or, rather, two witnesses who attend the ceremony along with other guests? Other guests can also attend the marriage ceremony. Was that the case when Milan Lukic got married?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had taken my son to receive an injection. He was -- had the flu. And when I was at the bridge, Milan caught up with me by car and he says, "Where are you going?" I said, "I'm taking Nikola, my son, to have an injection." And he said, "Well, come on. When you finish that, be my kum at my wedding." And I said, "I'm not ready for anything like that." You have to have a ring or anything. I didn't have any money, either. And he said, "Don't worry about a thing. You don't need anything. I have the rings." So what could I do? I couldn't say no. I had to do it. So we went to the hospital. My son received an injection. I went home, and he said, "I'll be there in half an hour." Well, I tidied myself up, changed my clothes. We went to the municipality building and there was only the registrar. I don't need to say the names. Or, rather, there was this person representing the municipality. I can't remember the name, what they're called. He's the main person on behalf of the municipality. There was me, and there was a little girl, Vidakovic, the kum of Vidakovic and his wife. We didn't stay there longer than five minutes. We just gave their particulars, signed it. We went to have lunch in a nearby restaurant. That was all. So it wasn't really a proper wedding ceremony. He did give me the rings, and I gave the rings to the registrar, and his wife. I felt rather uncomfortable having to do that because I didn't have the rings. So if I was kum, I would have -- actually, I should have bought the rings, but I didn't have the money and he had the rings. He probably knew I didn't have the money to buy the rings with, so he supplied the rings. And that's how it went. The wedding was over in a flash. I don't know. I wasn't -- I didn't want to turn him down. That would have been a pity. Now I know that -- what we should have done, according to custom, but that's how it was. And I christened their child as well. I was kum at the christening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The rings that you say is customary for the kum to buy, the kum usually buys the rings and brings them, but you say on this occasion, he bought the rings and gave them to you to hand over; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And had I knew ten days earlier, I would have done this myself. You know why he was in a hurry, because his wife was supposed to give birth. She was just about to give birth, so that's why everything was done so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that day in the municipality, there was just the registrar, that is to say, the employee of the municipality, the person conducting the wedding ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But the person representing the municipality, the lady conducting the wedding ceremony, myself, and this little girl and who was the kuma to his wife, to the bride. She was the daughter of a friend. So she was the little kuma to the bride. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you make pauses, please, between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Domazet? Please pause before you ask the question, and Mr. Vasiljevic, will you please pause before you answer. It seems so long ago since we had to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say "girl." She would have had to have been of age to have been a witness, I suppose, and she was the second witness at the wedding ceremony; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So your wife didn't attend the ceremony, did she?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the two of us, and the registrar, and the employee of the municipality, representing the municipality. The deputy or whatever he's called, and the registrar was a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that, you say you went to have lunch, those same people? Those two and you two as kums?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that customary, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a wedding, you usually have a big wedding and you invite your friends and family and lots of other things, you have neighbours. But in this particular case, he didn't organise anything else because his wife was just about to give birth. So he organised this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Vasiljevic, how much time went by from that day to the day when you christened their child, approximately, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she was two and a half. I think in 1980 she was christened, that's what I think. Maybe at the -- I don't know, thereabouts. She was big.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: She had already started walking.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, she was two and a half years old, more than two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I understand you to say that the girl was two or two and a half, but could you have a look at the transcript. It can't be that year, all it can be is a mistake there, because as I see, and you did say 1980. You said 1980, which would make it 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise. 1998, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Milan Lukic have a ceremonious lunch or dinner to mark the occasion as is customary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did your wife attend?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, asked by Mr. Groome about Milan Lukic and the people who were with him, when it comes to how this group was called, the name of the group, you, at one point, said that it was called the "Chetnik Movement," the "Cetnicki Pokret"; is that correct, and if so, how did you hear of that or were there other names that the group was given or did they -- is that how they called themselves?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, yes, Cetnicki Pokret or Chetnik movement, I don't know. The witnesses said the White Eagles. I never heard of that. I haven't -- didn't hear of the White Eagles, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the term "osvetnik" or "avenger"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave that name to the group later on. I know they had a flag with the avengers or something like that, osvetnik, but I was on sick leave. I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Asked by Mr. Groome about whether you recognised anybody in Pionirska Street on the 14th of June, apart from (redacted) whom you sat down with, you looked at the list and said -- and gave us a few names. Amongst them, you mentioned VG61. Would you take a look at the list, please. And you said you saw part of his statement. Now, did you see that witness personally, and if you did, did you talk to him, or do you only assume that he was there in view of the statement he gave?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know what I said. Perhaps I didn't say it properly, but I meant his father. He was on the cassette, on the tape. I didn't see him, I saw his father, that's who I meant, on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise to you. Yes, I was thinking of the elderly person, the father.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said the father. That's who I meant, (redacted), his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you saw that particular person on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The father?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did. He was a little fatter. I know him, but I don't know his name. He was on the photograph that they showed. [redacted], but I forgot his first name. The witness mentioned it but I didn't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the list and see VG115, you also said something in response to Mr. Groome's question, is that the person who was with the group from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw her ever. That is to say I did see her in Visegrad, but not that day. I don't know anything about that day, not that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does this mean, Mr. Vasiljevic, that Witness VG115 you did not see on that day in Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing her at all at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I seem to remember that you mentioned a witness whom you had seen, that's why I'm asking you. So if I ask you once again: Are you certain, did you see that person in Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen her. I don't know what I said. Maybe I mixed something up, mixed things up, but she says that she saw me the whole of June. I was in the hospital. She says Bikovac and Pionirska so there's something not right there, but I know her well and if I did see her, I did not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One of Mr. Groome's questions was the direction from the hotel in the centre of town to Pionirska Street. The question was whether you had seen anybody on that road on the way. Now, my question is: From the hotel in Visegrad going towards Pionirska Street, do you have to cross the bridge across the Rzava River?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, from that bridge to the hotel in Visegrad, are there one or more directions that you can take?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Rzava Bridge to the Visegrad Hotel, well, you can go via the Drina, there is a road, or you can take the road through the centre, so there are several ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So from the Visegrad Hotel to the Rzava Bridge, there are at least two independent routes you could take; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From the Rzava Bridge to Pionirska Street; is that the same case or just one route?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just one road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said that you came across the horse, you found the horse up above Pionirska Street, you said that the horse was tied, tethered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Groome's question was: Why did you go to fetch the horse in the first place, because he says that the horse could have survived where he was. Did you know that the horse was tied? Did the person who sent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you there tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when I got there, I saw that he was tied up, and he had trodden on the grass all around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you knew horses very well. Could he have survived had he remained tethered like that and had nobody to come and take him away?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because a horse needs water and food. But somebody would have come by and untied him, somebody could have come by and untied him. But tied up as he was, he wouldn't have survived. I'm sure somebody would have come by and saved him at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Asked by Mr. Groome about what you intended to do with the horse, you used an expression several times which, in Serbian, you said, you used the term "odbiti," and the interpreters translated this word "odbiti" "refused," but that has no logic. Would you explain what the Serbian term you used "odbiti" means when you wanted to say that you --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to point the horse towards this area so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it's got nothing to do with "refuse," it means to point the horse in a direction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 9.30 in the morning.
